201.dq: stress generally falls on the second to the last syllable of the underlying root. Thus, the accented syllable remains fixed on the second to the last syllable of the root, regardless of the addition of prefixes or suffixes.
201.dloc: Laidig & Laidig 1991 Tarus Sou Rikedu (Larike Grammar) p.26; also p.43 "independent pronouns with penultimate word-level stress"; StressTyp2 entry PDs 648/649/650 pdomain=root + entry (Laidig 1992) "always associated with the underlying penultimate syllable of the root"
201.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the underlying root and does not shift with prefixation or suffixation (ana-na ['ʔanana] vs anana [ʔa'nana]; pa-kadi-ku [pa'kadiku] vs paka-diku [paka'diku]); root-final VV counts as two nuclei ([pa'tae]); epenthetic -u/-e are extrametrical; in contractions/compounds stress goes to the underlying penult of the right-most root.
201.srule: Secondary stress (C. Laidig 1992, as excerpted in StressTyp2; the 1995 synopsis and 1991 grammar are silent): after primary is placed on the penult of the underlying root, secondary stress alternates, falling on the second (and fourth) surface syllable away from the primary, to its left or right.
201.quote: To assign word stress in Larike, it is necessary to have access to the underlying root. The general stress rule is that stress is always associated with the underlying penultimate syllable of the root; stress does not shift with affixation. It should be emphasized that the underlying penultimate syllable is not always the same as the surface penultimate syllable. For example, there are several roots that contain a final VV sequence, such as [pa'tae] 'to leave' where the VV sequence is pronounced as a surface diphthong. Therefore, [pa'tae] is realized on the surface as a two-syllable word, app…

201.exq_: A detailed treatment of stress placement, along with a discussion of apparent exceptions to the general rule of stress placement is found in C. Laidig (1992). ... [pa'tae] is realized on the surface as a two-syllable word, apparently receiving stress on the ultimate syllable.

morph.rootq: "To assign word stress in Larike, it is necessary to have access to the underlying root. The general stress rule is that stress is always associated with the underlying penultimate syllable of the root; stress does not shift with affixation. It should be emphasized that the underlying penultimate syllable is not always the same as the surface penultimate syllable." (Sec.2.6, p.23). Also: epenthetic -u/-e "is not ... part of the underlying root, it does not affect penultimate syllable stress on the root (i.e., /-u/ is extrametrical)" (Sec.2.7, p.24); in contractions/compounds "primary stress falls on the surface syllable containing the underlying penultimate syllable of the right-most root"…
morph.elicq: The synopsis does not say how stress was determined; stress examples are single words with phonetic transcriptions (exx. 1-12), and the detailed evidence is deferred: "A detailed treatment of stress placement, along with a discussion of apparent exceptions to the general rule of stress placement is found in C. Laidig (1992)." (p.24). On data generally: "Data for this paper have been collected over a four year period from 1988 to 1991 in the village of Larike." (note 1, p.40). The one text is "transcribed and edited from a cassette recording of a native speaker" (Sec.8, p.37) but stress is not marked in it ("Word stress is also not marked", note 10).
morph.stmt: Mixed but prefix-heavy on the verb and possessed noun: subject agreement (Set I), realis/irrealis/negative, causative pa-, stative n- and possessor markers are prefixes, while object agreement (Set II), completive -e, transitive -ku, noun plural -i/-u, nominaliser -ta, genitive -na/-ri and reciprocal -duma are suffixes — "There are three mutually exclusive prefixes which occur immediately following the subject prefix... the negative morpheme ta-, the irrealis morpheme na-, and the realis morpheme i-... Other common verb prefixes include the causative morpheme pa- 'CA' and the stative marker n- 'ST', which occur immediately preceding the verb root. Verb suffixes include the transitive…

qtr.text: §11. The word accent is strongly expiratory and usually rests on the first syllable, which is why it is not marked in writing. The compounds too have the accent on this syllable; e.g. ... pazinu 'I knew', nepazinu 'I did not know', ... jadzer 'one must drink'. ... In Latvian, then, initial stress prevails, whereas the other Baltic languages have preserved the free word accent (with certain restrictions)

202.sec_rule: Secondary stresses exist (Endzelin: 'Auch Nebenakzente gibt es außer dem Hauptakzent') and are quantity-conditioned: in disyllables the final syllable is secondarily stressed if suffixal or long (or a short root syllable after a short prefix, ne·sìt); in trisyllables a long syllable in an iambic or trochaic ending bears it (ádatā̀m, lábī̀ba), otherwise none is clearly heard; in 4-5-syllable words it follows the listed quantity patterns, typically on the third syllable (ádatìņa, méitenī̀te, lásītā̀ji); in words of five or more syllables it is less stable. (Kariņš 1996: moraic trochees L->R in 2-3-syllable words, syllabic trochees L->R in 4-5-syllable words, stem-stressed exceptions.)
202.sec_quote: Auch Nebenakzente gibt es außer dem Hauptakzent. In zweisilbigen Wörtern ist die Endsilbe nebentonig, wenn sie suffixal oder lang ist [...]. In dreisilbigen Wörtern hat einen deutlichen Nebenton die Länge in einem jambischen oder trochäischen Ausgang (z. B. D. Pl. adatäm; N.S. labība) [...]; sonst ist bei gleicher Quantität der zwei letzten Silben [...] kein deutlicher Nebenton zu hören.

secx.sec_quote_tr: There are also secondary accents besides the main accent. In disyllabic words the final syllable bears secondary stress if it is suffixal or long [...]. In trisyllabic words a long syllable in an iambic or trochaic ending has a clear secondary stress (e.g. dat. pl. adatām; nom. sg. labība) [...]; otherwise, when the last two syllables are of equal quantity, no clear secondary stress is heard.

tn.quote: § 14. Intonationen. ... Seit der urlettischen Zeit hat man es zunächst mit drei Intonationen zu tun: der gestoßenen, fallenden und gedehnten, und zwar sowohl bei langen Vokalen und Diphthongen, als auch bei Verbindungen von kurzen Vokalen mit tautosyllabischem r, l, m, n. ... Der Stoßton wird hier mit ^ bezeichnet, z. B. rîts 'Morgen' ... Diese drei Intonationen finden sich beisammen nur noch in einem Teil der mittellettischen Mundarten ... Die drei Intonationen werden nur unter dem Wortakzent streng voneinander geschieden.
tn.translation: §14. Intonations. ... Since Proto-Latvian times one has, to begin with, three intonations to deal with: the broken, the falling and the sustained ('drawn'), and this both on long vowels and diphthongs and on combinations of short vowels with tautosyllabic r, l, m, n. ... The broken tone is marked here with ^, e.g. rîts 'morning' ... These three intonations are found together only in a part of the Central Latvian dialects ... The three intonations are strictly kept apart only under the word accent.
tn.cite: Endzelin, J. 1923. Lettische Grammatik. Heidelberg: Carl Winter. I. Lautlehre, 2. Betonung, §11 Wortakzent (pp. 17-20), §14 Intonationen (pp. 21-24), §15 (pp. 24-25)
tn.note: Three syllable intonations (broken ^, falling `, sustained ~) on long vowels, diphthongs and V+r/l/m/n, beside fixed initial expiratory stress; fully distinct only under stress; most dialects keep 2.

evidence_works.work: Kariņš 1997, Lexical tone and stress in Latvian (Proceedings of the 23rd Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 23: 186-197)
evidence_works.detail: Primary-stress statement restates Endzelins 1922 ('Main word stress in Latvian occurs on the first syllable of a word (see Endzelins, 1922)', p.186). First-hand instrumental part: F0 (pitch) contours and durations for three speakers of the middle dialect; duration of /i:/ in mi:fi (level), gri:da (falling), dzi:ve (broken) for three speakers (fig. 9, p.189); pitch contours of the diphthong /ie/ under the three tones in primary-stressed vs non-primary-stressed syllables, speaker JP (figs. 10-11); and fig. 12, the short stressed vowel /a/ in nekad 'never' from speaker IL, a 48-year-old male from Riga, showing that 'a rise in pitch occurs over the primarily stressed syllable even if this syllable is non-initial' (p.189). Phonological reading: primary stress is associated with a H tone, represented in (16) for vaga 'furrow' (stress on the first syllable) and nekad 'never' (primary stress on the second syllable) (p.193); the three-way tonal contrast holds on all heavy syllables 'regardless of main word stress' (p.186), consistent with tone_cls 'tone-and-stress'.

excx.exc_elsewhere_quote: In Laz, stress is regularly penultimate in non-verbs (Marr 1910: 4; Öztürk & Pöchtrager 2011: 18). In verbs, stress is rightmost in the part of the stem up to and including the perfective causative marker; all suffixes following the perfective causative marker are stress-repelling. If there is no perfective causative marker, stress is placed as far right as possible, excluding the stress-repelling affixes. 205.dq: In phrases and sentences, each word maintains its own internal stress pattern, but primary stress occurs only once in the string. Thus the last primary-stressed vowel retains primary stress, while all other occurrences of primary stress reduce to secondary stress, and all occurrences of secondary stress reduce to tertiary stress
205.dloc: Lynch 1978:19 (PL B-55), §2.4.1 'Stress', before example (56); p.19 also: 'In polysyllabic verbs and adjectives of four or more syllables, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable; secondary stress falls on the initial syllable...'
205.prule: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of polysyllables (monosyllables are stressed). Stated exceptions: words ending in a geminate vowel cluster (+C), glide+C or glide+h, the transitive postclitic -ɨn word-finally, and certain acute-marked morphemes take final stress; a few acute-marked words (e.g. nákapun 'fishing-net') take antepenultimate stress.
205.srule: Secondary stress is obligatory and split by word class: verbs and adjectives of four or more syllables take secondary stress on the initial syllable and on alternate syllables to its right, never on the syllable before the penultimate primary (5 syll. 10010, 7 syll. 1010010); other polysyllables (nouns) take it on every alternate syllable to the left of the penult (5 syll. 01010, 7 syll. 0101010). In phrases non-final primaries reduce to secondary.
205.quote: Stress in Lenakel is generally of an alternating pattern, and falls on the vowel as the nucleus of a syllable. The vowel in a monosyllable receives primary stress, as does the penultimate syllable in a polysyllable. [...] In polysyllabic verbs and adjectives of four or more syllables, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable; secondary stress falls on the initial syllable; and secondary stress also falls on each alternate syllable to the right of the initial syllable, except that the syllable immediately preceding the primary-stressed syllable never receives stress.
205.idn: the south-western Lenakel dialect, the 'standard' dialect used by the Presbyterian Mission ('that outlined here is spoken natively in the south-west of the Lenakel-speaking area'); Lenakel described as a dialect complex within a chain with North Tanna and Whitesands; data: central west of Tanna island, Southern…
205.exq_: There are certain regular exceptions to the rules outlined above. Words ending in a geminate vowel cluster followed optionally by a consonant, or in a glide + consonant cluster, or in a glide + h, take final and not penultimate primary stress.

205.sec_rule: Two rules by word class (Lynch 1978:19; 1974:182-185): verbs and adjectives take secondary stress on the initial syllable and on every alternate syllable to its right, except that the syllable immediately before the primary-stressed penult is never stressed; nouns, adjuncts and other polysyllables take secondary stress on every alternate syllable to the left of the primary-stressed penult (initial syllable not necessarily stressed). Final-stressed polysyllabic verbs: secondary stress on the antepenult and the initial syllable, alternating between them (1978:20).
205.sec_quote: In polysyllabic verbs and adjectives ... secondary stress falls on the initial syllable; and ... on each alternate syllable to the right of the initial syllable, except that the syllable immediately preceding the primary-stressed syllable never receives stress. ... In other polysyllables, every alternate syllable to the left of the primary-stressed penultimate syllable receives secondary stress

Both initial and post-initial stress is found in words with closed initial syllables' - i.e. a closed initial syllable licenses lexical variation, not a determinate rule.

207.tone: Two contrastive (phonemic) tones, high (acute) and low (unmarked); each syllable bears a tone; lexical minimal pairs (/ngai/ L-H-H 'I, me' vs /ngai/ L-L-L 'sourness'); the majority of speakers, incl. the described Kinshasa model speaker, use tone; a sub-population uses (mostly penultimate) stress instead of tone; unassimilated French loans usually take a final high tone; statements vs questions by sentence intonation (Note 1.7).

tn.quote: Lingala, like almost all the languages spoken south of the Sahara,is a tone language. Each syllable has its own tone. Tone is as much an integral part of a syllable as vowels and consonants. Words are distinguished by tone, e.g., /ngáí/, 'I', 'me' (a low and two highs), and /ngai/, 'sour(ness)', 'bitter(ness)' (three lows). Lingala has two contrastive or phonemic tones: high /´/, low / / (unmarked). However, there are many speakers of Lingala who use a stress system instead of tones. Most speakers who use a stress system stress the penultimate syllable.
tn.cite: Redden, James E., F. Bongo & associates. 1963. Lingala: Basic Course. (Foreign Service Institute Basic Course Series, ed. Carleton T. Hodge.) Washington, D.C.: Foreign Service Institute, Department of State (ERIC ED 010 481).
tn.note: Two level tones, high (acute) and low (unmarked), one on every syllable; words contrast by tone alone; many speakers use penultimate stress instead of tone; sentence pitch drifts downward.

207.cfw: The penultimate-stress record rests on one aside in Redden & Bongo 1963, a teaching course that itself calls Lingala a two-tone language and attributes penultimate stress only to some speakers who do not use tone, while Meeuwis 2013 and Meeuwis 2019 describe lexical and grammatical tone with minimal pairs and no word stress at all.

208.dq: In citation forms stress falls on the last syllable of nouns. In context stress is always retracted to the penult. If the penult is a short epenthetic, stress is antepenultimate. In verbs, the last vowel of the root is usually stressed (Khan 19 :70).

208.prule: Primary stress on the final syllable of the word, which Khan (1999:70) calls the basic position (citation forms of nominals are stressed on the final syllable); in many nominals the stress is retracted to the penult, or to the antepenult when the penult vowel is a short epenthetic (pp. 70-71), and in verbs it falls on the last syllable of the root (past base, imperatives) or the first syllable of the inflectional suffix (present base), further suffixes usually leaving it in place (pp. 72-73, 118). StressTyp2's penultimate coding is not Khan's statement.

208.cfw: Khan's 1999 grammar of the Jewish dialect of Arbel names the end of the word as the basic stress position (citation forms of nouns are stressed finally, with retraction to the penult in connected speech), and Kim 2008, drawing on Khan 1999 and on Mutzafi 2004 for Koy Sanjaq, likewise lists Arbel and its sister dialects among the final-stress dialects, so the penultimate rule shown here, which follows the StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz and van der Hulst 2015) paraphrase of Khan, is the weaker reading and the record should be read as final stress with contextual retraction.

209.dq: With the exception of a few monosyllabic words that may be unstressed in the sentence, a word has at least one stressed syllable. The primary stress in Livonian is on the first syllable of a word. This is valid also for foreign words. ... If a prosodic word has four or more syllables, the secondary stress is usually on the third syllable of a word
209.dloc: Tuisk 2015:177-178, StressTyp2 entry (Hayes 1995:200) "Main stress is initial, secondary stress on third, tertiary stress on fifth syllable. Vowel length is phonemic.... The secondary tertiary contrast is possibly due to intonational downdrift."
209.prule: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word, in foreign words too; only short-syllable verb prefixes borrowed from Latvian can be unstressed (stress then on the stem-initial syllable), while long-syllable prefixes are stressed like the stem (Tuisk 2015:177).
209.srule: Secondary stress usually on the third syllable in words of four or more syllables; in words of five or a larger odd number of syllables the secondary-stressed foot is usually trisyllabic (final syllable unstressed). Exceptions: the affix -nikā takes secondary stress on the second syllable; long-vowel non-initial syllables of late loanwords can bear secondary stress (Tuisk 2015:177-178).
209.quote: With the exception of a few monosyllabic words that may be unstressed in the sentence, a word has at least one stressed syllable. 209.tone: Livonian distinguishes two tones in stressed stem-initial syllables, the plain tone and the broken tone or stød (Tuisk 2015:180); the article does not analyse the tonal contrast, and its stress-placement rule (pp. 177-178) is stated without reference to tone.

209.sec_rule: Secondary stress usually on the third syllable in words of four or more syllables (pie·dāgõ:dõn 1010); trisyllables form a single foot with no secondary stress (100); in words of five or a larger odd number of syllables the secondary-stressed foot is usually trisyllabic, leaving the final syllable unstressed (o·pāti:jizõn 10100). Lexical exceptions: the affix -nikā carries secondary stress even as the second syllable (mȯ·izni:kā); non-initial long-vowel syllables of late loans may carry secondary stress (ka·ptē:n); compound members keep their own stress.
209.sec_quote: If a prosodic word has four or more syllables, the secondary stress is usually on the third syllable of a word (pie·dāgõ:dõn ’pine, DPl’). If a word has five syllables or a larger odd number of syllables, the secondary-stressed foot is usually trisyllabic (o·pāti:jizõn ’teacher, DSg’). However, in the derivational affix -nikā the secondary stress can be on the second syllable of a word

evidence_works.detail: Livonian is described as having five quantity–stød foot templates: strong templates strengthen the stressed syllable's coda by consonantal overlength (Q3) or by stød, a glottal prosody confined to heavy stressed syllables, in complementary distribution, while weak templates lack both and keep or lengthen the post-stress vowel. The entry's initial stress and plain-vs-broken-tone note are consistent; the paper treats stød as a laryngeal prosody rather than a tone and adds its distribution and origins (former syllable boundary, lost *h).

tn.quote: The primary stress in Livonian is on the first syllable of a word. ... Livonian differentiates two tones in stressed stem-initial syllables — the plain tone and the broken tone or stød. Studies on Livonian tones have shown that the duration of the stressed syllables in words with stød is usually smaller than the syllable duration in words with the plain tone (e.g. Teras, Tuisk 2009). In the current study this pattern is not analyzed, but the question of a similar tendency in words longer than two syllables is definitely intriguing.

210.dq: Im Sorbischen wird wie im Čechischen ganz allgemein jedes Wort auf der ersten Silbe betont, wenn es auch noch so viel Silben zählt ... Ausser dem Hauptton auf der ersten Silbe besitzen in den meisten Gegenden des Niedersorbischen ... drei- und mehrsilbige Wörter einen Nebenton auf der vorletzten Silbe
210.prule: Main stress (Hauptton) on the first syllable of every word, whatever its length (Mucke 1891 §82.1); where a penultimate Nebenton co-occurs, the initial stress is the primary one.
210.srule: Per Mucke 1891 §82.2, in most areas of Lower Sorbian (and the Muskau dialect, partly the eastern border dialect) words of three or more syllables carry a secondary stress (Nebenton) on the penultimate syllable, which as a rule lengthens it and is more marked the longer the word (trisyllables included, e.g. cërwjóny); toward the eastern language border the Nebenton strengthens and can outrank the initial main stress (§82.3).
210.quote: § 82. Das allgemeine Gesetz der Betonung im Sorbischen. 1. Der Hauptton. Im Sorbischen wird wie im Čechischen ganz allgemein jedes Wort auf der ersten Silbe betont, wenn es auch noch so viel Silben zählt, z. B. dròga ... 2. Der Nebenton. Ausser dem Hauptton auf der ersten Silbe besitzen in den meisten Gegenden des Niedersorbischen, des Muskauer und teilweise auch des östlichen Grenz-Dialects drei- und mehrsilbige Wörter einen Nebenton auf der vorletzten Silbe, durch welchen diese in der Regel eine gedehnte Aussprache erhält, die um so deutlicher hervortritt, je länger das Wort ist
210.loc: Kap. XIII 'Betonung', §82.1-2, p. 148, read; the chapter opens (same page) 'Einen beweglichen Accent, wie das Russische, Südserbische und Kaschubische besitzt die lausitzisch-sorbische Sprache nicht mehr.'
210.idn: niedersorbische Volkssprache 'in allen ihren Localmundarten einschliesslich der Grenzdialecte' plus the Schriftsprache; the stress statement itself is qualified regionally ('in den meisten Gegenden des Niedersorbischen, des Muskauer und teilweise auch des östlichen Grenz-Dialects'; eastern border villages Horno/Rogow…
210.exq_: Bei dem Superlativpraefix ns. nëj- ... ist ... die Betonung schwankend, d. h. es kann entweder nëj- (naj-) oder die erste Silbe des gesteigerten Adjectivs den Ton erhalten ... Werden dieselben aber noch als Fremdwörter gefühlt ..., behalten sie auch den Accent ihrer Sprache: karéjta ... proféta

210.sec_rule: Secondary stress (Nebenton) on the penultimate syllable of words of three or more syllables, the penult being as a rule lengthened and the Nebenton more prominent the longer the word (cěrwjôny, Lùbošcâński, pòwołânjë, pòdrožnikôjstwo, dòhupśipadôwaś); regional ('in den meisten Gegenden'), strongest toward the east; none in disyllables (Mucke 1891:148 §82.2-3, 150 §83.4). Kaulfürst 2019:8-9 (own recordings, dialect texts): this penult secondary in 3+-syllable words is facultative ([ˈzɛˌlʲɛnɨ], [ˈzabiˌjanʲɛ]) and not obligatory in the standard; Janaš 1984:56 (via Gordon 2002:507, the record's strings) restricts it to words of four or more syllables, which Kaulfürst fn. 11 corrects.

morph.rootq: General rule does not mention the root: 'Except in words of Anêm origin, stress tends to be penultimate, but in Anêm borrowings, the stress occurs on the same syllable as it does in the Anêm word pronounced in isolation.' (B-83 App. C p.93). For the /-ka-/ verb class the statement is relative to the prefix/stem boundary: 'Taken as a group, Lusi forms with /-ka-/ are characterised by numerous final consonants, by many consonant clusters uncharacteristic of basic Lusi phonology, and by stress on the syllable after the prefix rather than on the penultimate syllable where it normally occurs in Lusi.' (B-83 §4.5 p.66). Also: 'Stress is not attested as phonemic.' (said of Anêm, App. C p.92).
morph.elicq: 'Stress patterns in running speech have not been worked out in detail for most of the languages, but for words pronounced in isolation, stress is usually penultimate in all languages.' (Thurston 1987, B-99 §2.17 p.34, covering Lusi among the NWNB languages). B-83 App. C p.93 likewise anchors the exception class to citation forms: 'in Anêm borrowings, the stress occurs on the same syllable as it does in the Anêm word pronounced in isolation.'
morph.stmt: Thurston: 'Verbs occur with an obligatory prefix marking subject; no other word classes occur with prefixes.' morph.elicq: Horton 1949 itself could not be read (borrow-only); neither the verbatim p.18 sentence in StressTyp2 nor the SPA 1979 digest of pp.10-14 says how stress was observed (missionary-grammar impressionistic description; no mention of wordlists, frames, texts or measurements). Yukawa 1987, the open source actually read, describes tone not stress, from elicitation with one speaker: 'The linguistic informant who assisted him was Mr. Godfrey C. K. Kalyocha, a student of the University of Zambia' (p.1).
morph.stmt: Luvale is a typical prefixing-inflection Bantu language with suffixal TAM/mood endings and verb extensions: nouns are 'noun prefix + stem' with 'each class [having] its own shape for the noun prefix' (Yukawa 1987:2), and finite verbs follow templates such as 'Subject Prefix + a + (Object Prefix +) Verb Stem + ile' (Yukawa 1987:7), with negation adding prefix ka- plus sentence-final enclitic =ko (p.7-8), while applicative, causative and passive are suffixes (Horton 1949:6 apud SPA 1979) — so person, class/number, tense, negation, diminutive, infinitive and reflexive marking precede the root and aspect/tense endings, mood -e, extensions, the object 'suffix' and =ko follow it.

212.sec_rule: One secondary stress two syllables from the main stress: where more than two syllables follow the main stress the penult carries a secondary stress; in other, morphologically determined forms the main stress is penult and the secondary falls two syllables to its left. StressTyp2 codes this as iterative secondary stress on even-numbered syllables from the right (i2@2R); the summary it quotes attests only the penult + fourth-from-last pair, and Horton's pp. 10-14 have not been seen first-hand.

tr.text: Translation of the quoted passage (Sundermann 1913:205): "As regards stress, the main rule is: in polysyllabic words the stress lies almost exclusively on the second-to-last syllable. If a word is lengthened, the stress moves further along accordingly. The latter, however, is not the case when a personal pronoun in shortened form is attached to a word as a suffix. One says, e.g.: anakku, anaknu etc. — my child, your child (from anak — child)." (The Gudai 1985:19 quotation is already in English.)

evidence_works.detail: The article restates antepenultimate stress (initial in one- and two-syllable words) for Western Macedonian, matching the catalog rule, and adds the clitic facts: enclitics after tenseless predicates count for stress placement (DOnesi, doNEsi go, doneSI mi go), preverbal object clitics are normally outside the stress domain, but under negation ne or a wh-word they join an enlarged stress domain and can carry antepenultimate stress (ne GO vide), with penultimate placement when the verb is monosyllabic (ne mu GO dal, the Monosyllabic Head Effect). The Macedonian data are taken from Lunt 1952, Fr

corr.head: StressTyp2's coding matches the source only in part
corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Macushi: primary stress on the final syllable; secondary stress: Left, iambic, iterative, QS (v1)". The source gives: Rhythmic alternation short-long-short-long over V/CV syllables counted from the left of the word/phrase (even-numbered light syllables are long = stressed and lengthened); the final CV of a phonological phrase (bounded by pause) is always long and stressed; CVV, VC and CVC syllables are inherently long and the alternation restarts after them (erepamî V.CV̄.CV.CV̄ vs eerepamî V̄V̄.CV.CV̄.CV̄; waimuyamî CV̄V̄.CV.CV̄.CV̄). Abbott does not rank one stress as primary; StressTyp2 takes the invariant final as primary.

215.heavy: Syllables with a contrastively long vowel or a diphthong (CVV), and closed syllables (VC, CVC; the only codas are glottal ' and n), are 'inherently long' (long = stressed with vowel length) and reset the short-long alternation.
215.dflt: All-light V/CV strings: even-numbered syllables from the left are long/stressed plus the phrase-final syllable always: 01, 011, 0101, 01011, 010101, 0101011 (arimarakayamî)...
215.prule: Rhythmic alternation short-long-short-long over V/CV syllables counted from the left of the word/phrase (even-numbered light syllables are long = stressed and lengthened); the final CV of a phonological phrase (bounded by pause) is always long and stressed; CVV, VC and CVC syllables are inherently long and the alternation restarts after them (erepamî V.CV̄.CV.CV̄ vs eerepamî V̄V̄.CV.CV̄.CV̄; waimuyamî CV̄V̄.CV.CV̄.CV̄). Abbott does not rank one stress as primary; StressTyp2 takes the invariant final as primary.
215.srule: Rhythmic stresses, not ranked against the final stress by Abbott: counting V/CV syllables from the left of the word/phrase, every even-numbered light syllable is 'long' (stressed, vowel lengthened), i.e. short-long-short-long; CVV (long vowel or diphthong), VC and CVC syllables are inherently long/stressed and the short-long count resumes after them (erepamî V.CV̄.CV.CV̄ 'I arrive' vs eerepamî V̄V̄.CV.CV̄.CV̄ 'you arrive'; waimuyamî CV̄V̄.CV.CV̄.CV̄ 'rats'); the count runs across word boundaries within the pause-bounded phrase.

217.prule: As a rule main stress falls on the initial syllable of bisyllabic and most trisyllabic words ([ˈamɑx] 'house', [ˈrapuˌwɔx] 'forest'). Stress can only fall on a phonemic, non-reduced vowel: the epenthetic schwa is skipped ([təˈtɔr] 'I carry on back'), and schwa-initial trisyllables whose first full vowel is /i/ before [j] take main stress on the final syllable ([fəniˈja] 'woman'). In po- nominalisations main stress falls on the first full syllable of the stem ([poˈkɑx] 'burnt garden'); words of more than three syllables (e.g. compound nouns) take the main stress of their second member ([ˌpɔrˈmapuˌwo] 'sky'). Dol calls stress 'weakly phonemic, as it cannot be fully predicted' (doublets (46), unpredictable forms (47)).
217.srule: In trisyllabic words a secondary stress may be heard on the final syllable (optional: 'may be heard'; e.g. [ˈrapuˌwɔx] 'forest'); no secondary falls on schwa or on a syllable adjacent to the main stress. In words of more than three syllables (e.g. compound nouns) secondary stress falls on alternating syllables to the left and right of the main stress ([ˌaraˈmawiʔja] 'ixora sp.', [ˌpɔrˈmapuˌwo] 'sky'); in compound nouns the left secondary is the stressed syllable of the first member (p.93). Not an obligatory simplex-word rule, so no secondary is marked in the grid.
217.quote: Lexical stress in Maybrat seems to be weakly phonemic, as it cannot be fully predicted. However, some generalisations which predict stress can be made: stress can only fall on a phonemic, non-reduced V. As a rule, main stress, marked ‘ » ’, falls on the initial syllable of bisyllabic words, as illustrated in (40), and most trisyllabic words, as illustrated in (41). In trisyllabic words, a secondary stress, marked ‘«’, may be heard on the final syllable. (40) /a|max/ [»amAx] ‘house’ ... /a|ya/ [»aja] ‘water’ (41) /ra|pu|oh/ [»rapu«wçx] ‘forest’ /i|si|e/ [»isi/je] ‘sun’

tn.quote: There are, however, prominent differences in the suprasegmental systems of Karon and Maybrat varieties. Dol (2007: 38–39) describes Maybrat Ayawasi as having a weakly phonemic stress system … Maybrat Ayamaru is argued by Brown (1991) and Witanti (1992: 46–49) to have a phonemic stress. Karon, by contrast, is a tone language. … The appearance of the high tone in Karon rarely corresponds to a stressed syllable in cognate vocabulary in Maybrat varieties. Particularly problematic is that many Karon lexemes have no tone, whereas a stressed syllable is present in all Maybrat lexical words.
tn.cite: Schapper, Antoinette. 2025. One language or two? The arbitrariness of isolate classifications in New Guinea. In Salaberri, Krajewska, Santazilia & Zuloaga (eds), Investigating Language Isolates (TSL 135). John Benjamins. doi:10.1075/tsl.135.10sch (HAL author version hal-05459805)
tn.locator: §4.2 'Case study 2: Maybrat-Karon', p. 12 (HAL author version pagination)
tn.note: Not a tone language: Maybrat (Ayawasi, Ayamaru, Mare) has weakly phonemic word stress and no lexical tone; the divergent Karon (Miyah) variety, by contrast, has a privative high tone.

217.cfw: Dol 1999/2007 calls Maybrat stress weakly phonemic and only "as a rule" initial, listing doublets and unpredictable non-initial forms, and Brown 1991 finds phonemic stress on any syllable with minimal pairs, so initial stress is the clear default but the fixed-initial coding overstates both first-hand descriptions.

219.heavy: none: the source states no syllable-weight criterion at all; stress placement is given purely by syllable count (parity) and word class (auxiliaries in the Verb Complex). Note 7: 'Relative loudness, pitch and length were not measured mechanically in the analysis of stress.' ST1's ': rhythmically strong' refers to rhythmic beats, not weight.
219.dflt: not applicable (no weight); primary is always on syllable 1 or 2
219.prule: Two phonological-word types: (a) stress on the 1st syllable and every odd-numbered syllable after it; (b) stress on the 2nd syllable and every even-numbered syllable after it; the leftmost stress is primary. By word length: 1-2 syllables initial; 3 syllables usually 1st (2nd optional/emphatic, obligatory under sandhi in the Verb Complex); 4 syllables usually 1st, but tetrasyllabic auxiliaries obligatorily 2nd; 5 and 7 syllables always 2nd; 6 and 8 syllables 1st. I.e., except in trisyllables (usually 1st + 3rd), primary = leftmost of a right-to-left binary count (even-numbered syllables from the end).
219.srule: Secondary stress on every second syllable after the primary: 3rd, 5th, 7th when primary is initial (3-, 4-, 6-, 8-syllable words), 4th and 6th when primary is on the second syllable (5- and 7-syllable words, tetrasyllabic auxiliaries), 'in accordance with the rule that every second syllable is stressed'; marked with a grave accent in Birk's examples (álawàr, múnankàřa, wiříniwà).

qtr.text: § 13. Stress in the Mansi word always falls on the first syllable; the following odd-numbered syllables carry secondary stress. The vowels of the first syllable are stressed; they are always strong, full, stable, and may be long or short. The vowels of non-first syllables are unstable [...] Thus word stress in Mansi is fixed: it falls on the first syllable. This stress extends also to words borrowed from Russian, e.g. u'chitel' 'teacher', pi'rkata 'brigade', ku'lup 'club', pe'karni 'bakery', i'skola 'school'.

221.dq: Main stress is initial; secondary stress on subsequent odd-numbered syllables. Sources differ on whether or not final syllables are stressed. (Hayes 1995:200)

221.quote: § 13. Ударение в мансийском слове всегда падает на первый слог, последующие нечётные слоги несут на себе второстепенное ударение. Гласные первого слога ударные, они всегда сильные, полные, устойчивые, могут быть долгими и краткими. Гласные непервого слога неустойчивые [...] Таким образом, словесное ударение в мансийском языке фиксированное, оно приходится на первый слог. Такое ударение распространяется и на заимствованные из русского языка слова, например: у‘чӣтель ‘учитель’, пи‘ркāта ‘бригада’, ку‘луп ‘клуб’, пē‘карни ‘пекарня’, и‘скола ‘школа’.
221.loc: § 13 'Ударение', pp. 38-39 (footnote 13 on p. 39: 'апостроф справа от гласного – это знак ударения')

221.exq_: According to Kálmán (1965: 31) the Tavda dialect of Mansi usually has stress on the second syllable in polysyllabic words. In the Konda and Pelymka dialects the stress is sometimes shifted away from the first syllable, although the circumstances under which this shift occurs are not specified.

morph.stmt: Manx is largely analytic: what bound inflection survives is mostly suffixal (plural -yn, future -ee/-ym, conditional -in/-agh, imperative pl. -jee, participle -it, verbal-noun and derivational suffixes), while the grammatical material in front of the root consists of unstressed proclitic particles written as separate words (article y/yn, possessives my/dty/e/nyn, negators cha/ny/nagh, aspect/VN particles er, dy), two segmental tense-aspect prefixes restricted to vowel-/f-initial verbs (past d-: iu > d'iu 'drank', fuirree > duirree; progressive g-: iu > giu 'drinking'), plus non-concatenative initial consonant mutation; Carmody 1947 p. 318: 'Except... with respect to a few genitives, there…

222.cfw: Broderick 1984, Green 1997 and Lewin 2020 all put Manx stress on the first syllable by default, but all three also describe a regular class of words in which a long second syllable draws the stress (mooarane, jarrood, the -ane/-age/-eyr suffixes and Anglo-Norman loans), so the default placement is secure while the 'strictly initial' label overstates what the sources say.

223.quote: 1.5 STRESS. Stress is non-phonemic in Maranungku, and falls on the first syllable of the word stem. Examples: /pán/, pan friend, mate; /tíralk/, tiralk saliva; /átʸawa/, atyawa urine. With words containing more than two syllables, a secondary stress falls on alternate syllables. Examples: /mǽræpæ̀t/, merepet beard; /ŋúriñmìn/, ngurinymin blackhead.

morph.rootq: "Stress is non-phonemic in Maranungku, and falls on the first syllable of the word stem. Examples: /pán/, pan friend, mate; /tíralk/, tiralk saliva; /átʸawa/, atyawa urine. With words containing more than two syllables, a secondary stress falls on alternate syllables. Examples: /mǽræpæ̀t/, merepet beard; /ŋúriñmìn/, ngurinymin blackhead." (§1.5, p.10). The statement is worded in terms of the 'word stem', but all five examples are monomorphemic nouns and nothing is said about stress on affix units, prefixes (wati-, wungku-, ka-/nga-) or suffixes.
morph.elicq: §1.5 (p.10) gives no method; the stress examples are single citation words with stress marks. The only statement about the evidence base is global (Introduction, p.vii): "Slightly more than 500 minutes have been recorded on tape. All of the material used in this description, with the exception of the verb pardigms [sic], is taken from spontaneous unelicited utterances by Maranungku speakers." (fieldwork Daly River July-Oct 1967 and March-July 1969).
morph.stmt: Lexical verb stems and nouns are essentially uninflected; bound verbal inflection is concentrated in a phonologically separate auxiliary, Tryon's 'affix unit' ("The affix unit consists of three morphemes... The first morpheme indicates the basic tense; the second indicates the person, and the third indicates the type of action", p.18; "The affix unit normally follows the verb stem and is phonologically separate from it", p.18, though "by far the most common ordering" in examples and texts is AU before verb stem, p.47), i.e. tense- and subject-prefixes before a class/aspect root, with object pronouns as "a series of suffixes to the affix units" (p.48) and reciprocal -nya suffixed (p.27)…

sources.text: "0.3 Rules and Processes 1. Stress is assigned by rule on the final vowel of the root. This is the same general rule found in other Yuman languages. Wares (1965:22) noted: \"Stress falls on the last syllable of the non-suffixed word in most Yuman languages and remains on the same syllable after suffixation.\" Some examples of stress assignment are [x6tIk] hot-k (good-real) [mox6tIk] ...". Corroboration: "Yuman languages regularly stress the final syllable of a word's root, which tends also to be word-final, and so words in Yuman languages typically exhibit word-final stress" (Geary 2022:1).

morph.rootq: "0.3 Rules and Processes 1. Stress is assigned by rule on the final vowel of the root. This is the same general rule found in other Yuman languages." (Gordon 1986:9; verbatim in StressTyp2 passage 1414 and in the OpenLibrary full-text fragment of the archive.org scan). Consistent detail p.7: "/r/ is an alveolar trill, which is also realized as a tap in pre-stress position"; the non-final suffixes -t-, -nt-, -pat-, -hot- and final -k/-m/-ma/-uum follow the stressed root vowel.
morph.elicq: The stress rule (p.9) is stated as a rule with no evidence base given. The grammar's data statement (Gordon 1986:5): "The data base for this grammar comes from several speakers of Maricopa. My primary teacher is Pollyanna Heath, with whom I have worked on a regular weekly basis since April 1977. We use standard elicitation techniques, collecting both isolated sentences and connected texts." No instrumental or frame-sentence evidence is mentioned for stress in the pages read.
morph.stmt: Gordon (1986:16, §1.1): the obligatory parts "of the verb are the pronominal prefixes, the verb root, and the final aspect-marking suffixes" — i.e. Maricopa has a short consonantal prefix field (person/possessor '-, m-, ny-, imperative k-, negative (w)aly-, reflexive proclitic mat, causative ch-/t-/uu-, nominalising uu-/kw-) before a stressed root, and carries case, demonstratives, number-of-possessor, negation -ma, non-final adverbials (-t-, -nt-, -pat-, -hot-, -haay) and all aspect/mood/switch-reference/interrogative marking as suffixes; in the 80-token sample suffix morphs outnumber prefix morphs 79:34, and because most prefixes are single consonants the orthographic-syllable ratio is…

morph.rootq: §2.5 pp.44-45 (3145): 'Stress in Wangkajunga is typical of other Western Desert languages, and Australian languages generally, in that the unmarked primary stress falls on the initial syllable. Primary stress is characterised by increased loudness. Secondary stress then falls on the second of the two following unstressed syllables. ... Clitics and suffixes are not part of the phonological word for stress assignment. Polysyllabic and disyllabic suffixes receive initial stress independently of the word stem. The stress pattern follows two rules. Firstly, primary stress should occur on the first syllable of as many morphemes as possible. Secondly, the…
morph.elicq: No method is stated for the stress description (§2.5). The word-level illustrations are unsourced ('The following examples of word level stress are illustrations. The stressed syllable is underlined.'), while clause examples carry text/notebook sigla and observations from recorded narrative, e.g. p.45: 'In example 2.18, although the speaker pauses before the sentence connective the primary stress still falls on the initial syllable of ngarlpurrima rather than on ka.' [DHN text]. General method §1.7.2 p.23: 'Initially I relied more heavily on information from the texts than eliciting forms.' No instrumental measurement is mentioned.
morph.stmt: Almost exclusively suffixing and encliticising: 'Nominals in Wangkajunga are made up of a lexical root, optional stem forming suffixes and, finally, the case inflection' (§3.1 p.54); verbs take derivational suffixes (§7.4-7.5), TAM/mood inflectional suffixes (ch.8) and post-inflectional suffixes (§7.7), with person/number/reflexive marked by a second-position enclitic bound-pronoun cluster 'attached to any class of word' (§6.2); the only prefixal elements are the verbal directional affixes: 'There are three directional affixes maa-, parra- and -ni. The former are affixed to the beginnings of verbs and -ni to the end' (§7.6 p.177; also wati- 'across').

225.sec_rule: Secondary stresses on non-final syllables after the initial main stress, left-to-right trochaic, with binary or optionally ternary spacing: 'In words of more than 4 syllables there is often a secondary stress on the third. In words of 5 syllables the position of the secondary stress varies' (Marsh 1969:146 apud StressTyp2); StressTyp2 secondary code 'Left, trochaic, iterative, ternary'; Hayes 1995:365-366 apud StressTyp2 'may have ternary stress... syllabic trochees, assigned from left to right'. No final-syllable stress. E.g. ˈwaɭpuˌkuřu ~ ˈyikařiwa (4σ), ˈwayinˌkatiŋu ~ ˈpakalkuˌɽaku (5σ), ˈkapuˌkuřiˌɳanta ~ ˈwuɽulaˌtjananja (6σ), ˈɳintiˌtjulaˌtjananja ~ ˈkayiliˌřiŋuˌlatju (7σ).

The morphological source (García García 2013) gives no description of word stress at all (tone only; 'acento' = orthographic tone diacritic), nor do Léonard & Kihm 2012 for Huautla.
morph.elicq: Pike 1948 gives no elicitation frame for the stress statement; the only provenance line (p. 4, same verified catalog record) is: "Huautla de Jimenez, Oaxaca. The data concerning it were gathered by me in collaboration with Miss Eunice Victoria Pike and Mrs. George Cowan, from 1936-45...". (García García 2013's own phonetic data — on tone, not stress — are isolated words: 'Los colaboradores emitían tres veces cada palabra' §1.3.2 p.5; his grammar examples 'provienen de grabaciones realizadas en conversaciones con personas de la comunidad' §2 p.10.)
morph.stmt: García García 2013:11 (Fig. 3, 'Templete verbal mazateco'): "PREFIJO — MARCA ASPECTUAL + RAÍZ VERBAL + MARCA DE PERSONA — SUFIJO"; p.14/p.38: "las marcas de persona... se pueden observar como sufijos fusionados a la raíz"; objects, dative subjects and alienable possessors are enclitics (=na, =li, =le...), nouns carry no case or number ('no existe número ni género gramatical', p.33), and derivation (causative/verbaliser) is by preposed preverbs/light verbs (s'ín-, b'é-; Patrón B p.37; Léonard & Kihm 2012: 'préverbe causatif sí-') — a head-marking language with TAM/mood and derivational material before the root and all person/possessor marking after it. 226.sec_quote: All the languages have two degrees of stress with heavy stress occurring on the last syllable of the stem; weak stress occurs elsewhere. Heavily stressed syllables are marked orthographically with acute accent over the vowel (or final vowel of complex syllable nuclei); weakly stressed syllables are regularly unmarked.

tn.quote: The basic tones of Mazateco are four. Each of these tones is phonetically level, within the limits of perception. ... (the highest tone is written with the numeral 1, the lowest with 4) ... When two different level tones are juxtaposed on a single syllable nucleus, they fuse to form a glide. The glide itself is not significant, but must be analyzed phonemically in terms of its beginning point and ending point. ... Clusters of two tones must be analyzed as sequences of two or three tone phonemes, rather than single but phonetically complex gliding tone phonemes
tn.cite: Pike, Kenneth L. & Eunice V. Pike. 1947. Immediate constituents of Mazateco syllables. International Journal of American Linguistics 13(2): 78-91.
tn.locator: IJAL 13(2), sec. 6 'Third and Fourth Divisions: Principal versus Subordinate Tones', pp. 87-88 (opening of sec. 6 and the glide statement) and p. 89 ('Clusters of two tones must be analyzed...')
tn.note: Four level tones (1 high... 4 low) borne by the syllable nucleus; 2-3 tones on one nucleus sound as glides but are tone sequences, mostly at fused suffixes. Final word stress stated separately. Checked against the source (tone consistency check round 3, 2026-09-24): floating unstated -> yes (IJAL 13(2), sec. 6, p. 88 and sec. 7, p. 90); evidence impressionistic -> alternations (IJAL 13(2), sec. 6, p. 89; paradigms p. 88 (si'ska! he plays + -a'... > si).

227.caution: Based on an excerpt only; the full text of the source has not been consulted.
227.dq: Dixon (1970, 1991) writes about Mbabaram (a language from the Cairns rainforest, near Cape York) that it usually stresses the first syllable that begins with a consonant, as in (25). Mbabaram does not have many trisyllabic words, but the pattern becomes clear from a comparison of some disyllabic words. (25) wánu 'termite', búmba 'ashes'; aŋál 'boomerang', albí 'grey'
227.dloc: Goedemans 1998, Weightless Segments (LOT Dissertations 9), ch. 5, p. 137 (full PDF from lotpublications.nl)
227.heavy: Dixon 1991: a closed second syllable bears stress (95%, with listed exceptions e.g. lángil); a long vowel is always stressed; a word-initial onsetless vowel /a/ never receives primary stress (V-initial disyllables must stress sigma-2). Gordon 2005 formalises this as the scale (C)VC > CV > V.
227.dflt: none stated -- C-initial disyllables with an open second syllable 'divide almost equally' between first- and second-syllable stress (lexical); V-initial all-light words take sigma-2
227.prule: Words are overwhelmingly mono- or disyllabic. V-initial (/a/-initial) disyllables: stress on sigma-2, obligatorily. C-initial disyllables: 'not predictable' -- if sigma-2 is closed it bears stress in 95% of cases (exceptions listed, e.g. lángil 'light'); if sigma-2 is open the words 'divide almost equally' between sigma-1 stress (búmba 'ashes', wunda 'not sweet') and sigma-2 stress (dambú 'short', dibú). A long vowel is always stressed. Monosyllables stressed. Trisyllables ('Only about a score of words have three syllables'): 'In most of these the second syllable is stressed' (yuwágil 'wind', alngída 'down hill', aráman 'woomera'); 'just four words in the corpus have primary stress' on the final syllable, with 'secondary stress on the first syllable' (gùridál 'eaglehawk', àrungúl 'kitehawk', gùludún 'dove', gùragán 'ironbark tree'); the only trisyllabic root with initial primary stress is mbábaram. Loans range over the same possibilities.
227.srule: Dixon 1991:360 (reached as an excerpt fragment only): trisyllabic words whose primary stress falls on the final syllable carry 'secondary stress on the first syllable: gùridál 'eaglehawk', àrungúl...'; the conditioning clause before the fragment was not reachable. Kager 1995:132, reporting Dixon 1991, agrees: most trisyllabic roots are stressed on the second syllable, 'some on the final syllable with an initial secondary stress' (gùridál, gùludún). Nothing on secondary stress in disyllables; StressTyp2 codes secondary 'No information'.
